FROM MY DESK   Weak. Despondent. Concerned. Those are a few of the words Democratic voters used to describe their party when we asked them to reflect on where things stand .

   With the midterm elections fast approaching, Democrats are on track to make gains in November, but they’re benefiting from President Trump’s unpopularity—not their own party’s image. In fact, Democrats have received some of their lowest approval ratings ever since Trump took office last year. 

   We brought together a group of Democratic voters from across the country to talk about the party’s trajectory, the rise of the DSA and who should lead the ticket in 2028. 

   In the coming weeks, we will also sit down with young men who voted for Trump in 2024 to see how they view the administration today.

   This is an edition of The 10-Point newsletter, a guided tour of the best coverage in The Wall Street Journal. If you’re not subscribed, sign up here . If you’re reading this in your inbox, tap the headline above for online and audio versions of this newsletter. 

       2. TODAY’S HEADLINES   • The near-disaster on FlyDubai Flight 1073 represents a major security failure that could weigh on the prospects of the U.A.E.’s aviation and tourism businesses.

   • The Pentagon is sending a third aircraft-carrier strike group and an additional Marine expeditionary unit to the Middle East as Trump considers renewing strikes on Iran after the midterms.

   • Explosive rape allegations have left Cornell’s campus reeling, with students demanding answers from the university’s administration.

   • Amazon is touting its good-neighbor bona fides in an attempt to shore up support for artificial-intelligence data centers.

   • Online sleuths known as “swarm chasers” are scouring the web for signs of rogue AI agents secretly communicating with one another, offering a rare look at how artificial intelligence can misbehave .

   • Stocks Spencer Jakab is watching: It would be hard to find a business harmed more by the double-whammy of high oil prices and a quarter-century peak in bond yields than one that sells recreational vehicles. Shares of leading RV dealer Camping World Holdings fell to a fresh 52-week low on Thursday. It is the stock’s lowest price on record except for a handful of days during the Covid-19 pandemic. That crisis had a silver lining as RV sales promptly surged, sending the stock up more than 1,000% in a year. History might not repeat. (Get Spencer’s Markets A.M. newsletter in your inbox .)

   • The monthslong rout in global government bonds is getting messier and weirder.

   • High government debt is adding fuel to the global bond-market selloff , writes Aaron Back.

       4. READ IT HERE FIRST   Michael Lewis tells the inside story of an epic DOGE standoff.   DOGE thought it could just walk in and take over the United States Institute of Peace—until security chief Colin O’Brien decided to block the way . In an exclusive excerpt from his forthcoming book, “Blockers,” Michael Lewis recounts the inside story of the high-stakes D.C. standoff where O’Brien fought off operatives for the department trying to argue their way into a building far removed from daily politics.

       5. REPORTER’S NOTEBOOK   Reporter Brenna T. Smith: What started as a simple question about local police performing federal immigration duties grew into a monthslong investigation. I was interested in how local police were getting deputized for immigration enforcement in the 287(g) program, which was phased out in 2012 and revived by Trump in 2025. It was really just a kernel of curiosity that, as we kept digging, bloomed into something much more specific.

I filed more than 350 public records requests with local law-enforcement agencies across the U.S. But when agencies join the program, their records become federal property. Local departments kept telling me to go to ICE, where requests sat unanswered.

My colleagues, Marianne LeVine and Jack Gillum, and I made a breakthrough. We found a public ICE fact sheet that contained data we boiled down to a reimbursement formula of how agencies were getting paid.

   We were surprised to discover payments are made per officer, not by performance. An agency can enroll dozens of officers, make few arrests and still collect millions in federal funds. Analyzing state and federal records, we confirmed this was happening in a few places. We also learned that many of the local law-enforcement agencies signing up for the task force were in sparsely populated areas with few immigrants.

Billions of dollars are being funneled toward this program without a comparable increase in local cops contributing to immigration arrests. For taxpayers, it raises the question: How effectively is that money actually being spent?

       8. THE NUMBER   9%   Believers in the AI boom need to take a very close look at this number: 9% of GDP. That’s how much American businesses and consumers eventually have to spend a year on the services of companies like Anthropic and OpenAI to justify the staggering sums being committed to the technology right now. Is it plausible that Americans will spend as much of their income on this one technology as they do on food? You should be skeptical, writes chief economics commentator Greg Ip.

       9. AND FINALLY…   Forget abs. Fit women now want to show off their biceps.   Eighty years ago Rosie the Riveter flexed her biceps in advertisements to encourage women to take manufacturing jobs during World War II. Today women are displaying their arm muscles once again, but this time it’s purely to show off how strong they are . Biceps have gotten so eye-popping that at least in one star-studded situation, they’re doubling for men’s.

1. FROM MY DESK

 

Weak. Despondent. Concerned. Those are a few of the words Democratic voters used to describe their party when we asked them to reflect on where things stand.

 

With the midterm elections fast approaching, Democrats are on track to make gains in November, but they’re benefiting from President Trump’s unpopularity—not their own party’s image. In fact, Democrats have received some of their lowest approval ratings ever since Trump took office last year.

This is an edition of The 10-Point newsletter, a guided tour of the best coverage in The Wall Street Journal. If you’re not subscribed, sign up here. If you’re reading this in your inbox, tap the headline above for online and audio versions of this newsletter.
